ai_summary: Scotland is currently operating with an ultra-clean generation mix, achieving a local carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh versus 89 gCO2/kWh GB-wide. Across the wider national network, GB wind output stands at 12.5 GW, driven significantly by an estimated Scottish wind output of 4.1 GW, which accounts for 40.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Despite this abundant renewable generation, structural transmission constraints across the boundary between Scotland and England prevent clean power from flowing south to primary demand centers. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 65.3 GWh through Balancing Mechanism bids, resulting in a constraint cost of about £3,638,946. To compensate for this lost zero-carbon electricity, thermal generators were dispatched elsewhere on the system, burning an estimated 12,398,621 m3 of gas elsewhere and emitting an additional 22,840 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere. Annualizing this daily run rate points to an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £1,328 million. When recovered across national electricity volumes, this balancing expense adds an estimated £5/MWh to everybody's invoice in the UK, highlighting the severe environmental and financial penalty of delayed grid expansion.
